Principles


The eight main points outlined in the Atlantic Charter


These foundational principles were forged in the aftermath of World War II, a time of great upheaval and uncertainty. The Atlantic Charter, a joint statement issued by the United States and the United Kingdom, represented a bold vision for a post-war world. It was a call to action, a promise to work together to build a brighter future for all nations and peoples.


The right of self-determination for all people


This fundamental principle is at the heart of the Atlantic Charter. It recognizes that every individual, every community, and every nation has the inherent right to determine its own destiny. This means that people should be free to choose their own path, to shape their own future, and to build their own societies.


In practical terms, this principle means that nations should be able to govern themselves, without external interference or coercion. It means that people should be able to live in peace, free from the threat of violence or oppression. And it means that nations should be able to work together, as equals, to address common challenges and achieve shared goals.


The commitment to disarmament and collective security


The Atlantic Charter also calls for a commitment to disarmament and collective security. This means that nations should work together to reduce the threat of war, to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons, and to promote a culture of peace.


In the aftermath of World War II, the world was still reeling from the devastating effects of conflict. The Charter recognizes that the only way to prevent such tragedies in the future is to work together, to build a system of collective security that would deter nations from going to war.


The promotion of economic cooperation and trade


Finally, the Atlantic Charter promotes economic cooperation and trade. This means that nations should work together to promote economic growth, to reduce poverty and inequality, and to build a more prosperous world.


In practical terms, this principle means that nations should be able to trade freely, without tariffs or other barriers. It means that people should be able to access the goods and services they need, without being held back by bureaucratic red tape or protectionist policies.


By promoting economic cooperation and trade, the Atlantic Charter recognizes that nations are stronger together. When nations work together, they can achieve far more than they could alone. They can build a more prosperous world, a world where everyone has the opportunity to thrive.
